Section 42(a) makes a violator 'liable for a civil penalty', but penalties are imposed by the Board (Section 33(b)) or recovered in a civil action (Section 42(d)), and injunction actions are brought by the State's Attorney or Attorney General 'at the request of the Agency' (Section 42(e)). (a) Except as otherwise provided in this Section, it shall be a Class A misdemeanor to violate this Act or regulations thereunder" ... "Sec. 42. Civil penalties. (a) Except as provided in this Section, any person that violates any provision of this Act ... shall be liable for a civil penalty" ... "(e) The State's Attorney of the county in which the violation occurred, or the Attorney General, may, at the request of the Agency or on his own motion, institute a civil action for an injunction" ... second_check.explanation: The finding holds. On the official ILGA text, Sec. 44 is headed 'Criminal acts; penalties', and 44(a) reads: 'it shall be a Class A misdemeanor to violate this Act...'. first_check.correct_citation: Castleberry v. Branscum, 721 S.W.2d 270, 271-73 (Tex. 1986); Lucas v. Texas Industries, Inc., 696 S.W.2d 372, 374-75 (Tex. 1984); SSP Partners v. Gladstrong Investments (USA) Corp., 275 S.W.3d 444, 451, 454-55 (Tex. 2008); Tex. Bus. Orgs. Code §§ 21.223, 101.002
first_check.explanation: No authority is cited, but the two-part statement is a fair paraphrase of Texas alter ego law for a tort claim: (1) unity such that the subsidiary's separateness has ceased, and (2) use of the entity to achieve fraud, injustice, or an inequitable result. Castleberry states alter ego applies when 'there is such unity ... that the separateness of the corporation has ceased and holding only the corporation liable would result in injustice'; Lucas requires 'something more than mere unity of financial interest, ownership and control' for a parent's liability for a subsidiary's tort; SSP Partners confirms the corporate form may be ignored only when used 'as part of a basically unfair device to achieve an inequitable result.' Section 101.002 extends the corporate veil-piercing provisions to LLCs. Two caveats: the 'no separate mind, will, or existence of its own' wording is instrumentality-rule phrasing (familiar from Ohio's Belvedere test) that did not appear in the Texas opinions read, and for contractual obligations sections 21.223(a)(2)/(b) and 101.002 require actual fraud for the direct personal benefit of the owner or affiliate, so 'injustice or inequity' suffices only for tort-type claims like the ones pleaded.
first_check.evidence_excerpt: Castleberry: "Alter ego applies when there is such unity between corporation and individual that the separateness of the corporation has ceased and holding only the corporation liable would result in injustice." Tex. Bus. Orgs. Code § 101.002(a): "Subject to Section 101.114, Sections 21.223, 21.224, 21.225, and 21.226 apply to a limited liability company and the company's members, owners, assignees, affiliates, and subscribers."

first_check.explanation: As history the sentence is literally true: Paramount Petroleum and other intermediate courts did recognize a single business enterprise theory where corporations 'integrate their resources to achieve a common business purpose.' But it is presented as what 'Texas law' recognizes, and the Texas Supreme Court squarely rejected that theory in 2008. SSP Partners held that 'corporations cannot be held liable for each other's obligations merely because they are part of a single business enterprise,' that the Court had 'never approved' the theory, that it is 'fundamentally inconsistent' with the Legislature's approach (now Tex. Bus. Orgs. Code § 21.223), and that it 'will not support the imposition of one corporation's obligations on another.' The petition's follow-on acknowledgment (para. 42) that 'certain Texas courts have questioned the continued independent viability' of the doctrine understates this: the state's highest court eliminated it as an independent basis for liability, leaving only veil-piercing theories that require abuse of the corporate form. The proposition as a statement of current Texas law is therefore contradicted by controlling authority.

SSP Partners itself says the theory was "put forward by the court of appeals in Paramount Petroleum" and that "other courts have applied the theory." The petition also concedes in para. 42 that courts have "questioned" the doctrine and pleads it to preserve the issue for appeal. But the sentence is framed as current "Texas law," and the Texas Supreme Court squarely rejected the theory in SSP Partners v. Gladstrong Invs. (USA) Corp., 275 S.W.3d 444 (Tex. 2008). The opinion (CourtListener 895058) says: "We also hold that corporations cannot be held liable for each other's obligations merely because they are part of a single business enterprise"; "The single business enterprise liability theory is fundamentally inconsistent with the approach taken by the Legislature"; and "we hold that the single business enterprise liability theory set out in Paramount Petroleum will not support the imposition of one corporation's obligations on another." As a statement of Texas law on a liability theory, the sentence is contradicted by controlling authority, and para. 42's word "questioned" understates an outright rejection. first_check.quote_check: "never expressly adopted": not found. The word "adopted" appears once in the opinion, in a footnote parenthetical about Restatement (Second) of Torts § 402A. The closest actual language is "We have never approved of imposing joint liability on separate entities merely because they were part of a single business enterprise" (275 S.W.3d at 452) and, in footnote 33 quoting PHC-Minden, "a theory we have never endorsed."
first_check.explanation: The case and reporter citation are correct (Tex. Nov. 14, 2008). The memo understates and partly misstates the holding. It says the Court 'declined to definitively abolish the SBE theory but expressed pronounced skepticism.' In fact the Court squarely held that corporations cannot be held liable for each other's obligations merely because they are part of a single business enterprise, and that the SBE theory set out in Paramount Petroleum 'will not support the imposition of one corporation's obligations on another.' The further statement that the Court said SBE 'conflates' veil piercing with enterprise liability is a loose paraphrase: no such wording appears, though the Court did reason that SBE lacks the abuse element veil piercing requires, that affiliated corporations may share control, purposes and finances without joint liability, and that SBE is inconsistent with the legislature's approach in former art. 2.21. The quoted phrase 'never expressly adopted' does not appear; the only hit for 'expressly' is in quoted former art. 2.21. The memo says the Court 'declined to definitively abolish' SBE.
